0.title: Defending and Commending the Christian Faith
0.essay:
Apologetics — from the Greek word for a formal defence in court — is the work of giving reasons for the Christian faith. It is less about winning arguments than about clearing obstacles so that people can see Christ.

A cultivated readiness

Its mandate comes from one of the most practical verses in the New Testament: “always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). Apologetics answers objections and makes the case that Christianity is true, coherent, beautiful and worth believing.

Every age, its questions

The church has always had its apologists: Justin Martyr, Augustine, Aquinas, Pascal, Butler, Paley, Chesterton, Lewis, Schaeffer, Sproul, Plantinga, Craig, Keller and many others. Each age needs its own apologetic, because each age raises its own objections. The first Christians argued for the resurrection against Jewish and pagan worldviews. The Enlightenment required a defence of Scripture’s rationality. Modernity raised the problem of evil and the supposed conflict with science. Postmodernity questioned truth itself. Our moment faces all of these at once, because objections do not go away; they accumulate.

A step into the light

The believer in the pew, and the questioner outside the church, need to know that Christianity is not a leap into the dark but a step into the light. It is not a retreat from reason, but the worldview that makes reason make sense. It is not a tribal comfort, but the truth about reality.

What this study covers

This study introduces the main approaches to apologetics, addresses the most common objections — the existence of God, the problem of evil, the resurrection, and the exclusivity of Christ — and trains believers in gentle, confident, gospel-centred engagement. Along the way we draw on C. S. Lewis, Francis Schaeffer, R. C. Sproul, Tim Keller, Alvin Plantinga, William Lane Craig, John Lennox and Greg Bahnsen.

The chapters

The Call to Defend: presuppositions and approaches. The Existence of God. The Problem of Evil. The Resurrection: the hinge of history. The Exclusivity of Christ. And Faithful Witness: apologetics as a way of life.

For reflection

What question about the faith do you find hardest to answer, whether it comes from others or from your own heart?

1.title: The Call to Defend: Presuppositions and Approaches
1.essay:
Everyone has a worldview: a set of foundational assumptions about reality, knowledge and value, whether or not they have ever examined it. Apologetics begins by bringing those assumptions to light.

Everyone has assumptions

The atheist assumes the natural world is all there is. The postmodernist assumes truth is culturally constructed. The moralist assumes there is a real standard against which lives should be measured. Apologetics asks whether these assumptions are coherent, and whether they can bear the weight placed on them.

Honour Christ first

The apologetic mandate sits in a passage about suffering. Peter writes to persecuted believers who must explain their hope in the face of hostility. And the first command is inward: “in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy” (1 Peter 3:15). The apologetic posture flows from the devotional one.

The second is preparation: “always being prepared.” Apologetics is not emergency improvisation but cultivated readiness. The third is mission: a defence “to anyone who asks.” And the fourth shapes everything: “with gentleness and respect.” The manner is not optional.

Answer each person

Paul adds, “Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Colossians 4:5–6). Not a one-size-fits-all argument, but a discerning response to the person in front of you: their questions, their culture, their real burden. Salt preserves and flavours. Apologetics that is technically correct but cold fails this test. Lewis, Chesterton and Keller are compelling not only because they are right, but because they are interesting, warm, and clearly love the people they address.

Francis Schaeffer insisted that the apologist must first earn the right to be heard: by listening, by understanding the questioner’s real burden, by responding to the person and not just the argument. The apologist who wins the argument but loses the person has failed.

What people already know

Romans 1 is foundational. “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth” (Romans 1:18). “For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them” (Romans 1:19).

So apologetics is not introducing God to a blank mind. It is uncovering what the mind already knows and has pushed down. Schaeffer called this “taking the roof off”: gently removing the shelter a person has built against the God they already know, and showing that it cannot keep out the weather of reality.

Paul in Athens

Paul’s speech to the Areopagus is the New Testament’s great apologetic address, and its method is instructive. He had walked their city and studied their culture. He began, “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious” (Acts 17:22). He found a point of contact: an altar “To the unknown god.” And then: “What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you” (Acts 17:23). He even quoted their own poets (Acts 17:28). He did not begin with denunciation, but with engagement. The gospel came, including a call to repent and the resurrection, but after careful, respectful listening.

Four approaches

The Reformed tradition produced the approach called presuppositionalism, developed by Cornelius Van Til and popularised by Greg Bahnsen. It argues that all reasoning takes place within a worldview, and that the Christian worldview — with its Creator God, image-bearing humans, objective truth and rational order — is the only one that can account for logic, science and morality. The unbeliever borrows from the Christian worldview every time they reason, make moral judgments or do science, and the apologist’s task is to show this.

Other approaches have real value. The classical approach of Aquinas, and of Sproul, argues from reason to God’s existence before turning to revelation. The evidential approach, as in Gary Habermas and Michael Licona, argues from historical evidence, especially for the resurrection. The cumulative-case approach of Lewis and Keller builds a convergent case from many lines of evidence. Most practitioners use elements of all four.

Reason and the Spirit

Presuppositionalism rests on the Reformed doctrine of the noetic effects of sin: sin has corrupted not just human behaviour but human reasoning. The unbeliever is not a neutral thinker who simply needs more evidence, but one who suppresses the truth. That does not make evidence irrelevant; Romans 1 says they already have the evidence of creation. But it means conversion needs the work of the Spirit, not just the presentation of arguments. The apologist prepares the soil; the Spirit gives life to the seed. Reformed apologetics is therefore always prayerful.

A question that opens

Think of a university student whose atheist professor dismisses her faith as irrational in an age of science. Instead of being flustered, she asks quietly: “When you say science shows there is no God, is that something science can prove, or something you believe? Science studies the natural world. Can it tell us whether there is a cause beyond the natural world?” The professor pauses. The conversation has moved from assertion to examination. She has not proved God’s existence, but she has opened a space for real thought. Often that is apologetics at its best: not an argument that closes a case, but a question that opens a mind.

For reflection

What assumptions do your friends and colleagues live by? What would it look like for you to honour Christ in your heart first, and then answer with gentleness and respect?

2.title: The Existence of God: Reason, Creation, and the Cosmological Case
2.essay:
Does God exist? This is the foundational question, and Christianity has never been afraid of it. The Christian claim is not “believe blindly and ask no questions,” but that God has made himself known to everyone who will honestly look.

The heavens are speaking

“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge” (Psalm 19:1–2). The psalm makes a remarkable claim. The heavens are not merely beautiful; they are communicating. And the message is universal: “There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard” (Psalm 19:3).

Everyone who has ever looked up at a starry sky has received this message. The apologist does not introduce people to evidence they have never seen. They help people understand the meaning of evidence they have been looking at all their lives.

Clearly perceived

Paul writes, “For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse” (Romans 1:20). Not dimly glimpsed, but clearly perceived. The problem is not insufficient evidence. It is suppression: a deliberate turning away from what is plain.

The witness of goodness

Paul told the crowd at Lystra that God “did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17). This is the argument from goodness: not only that the universe is ordered, but that it is good. Every meal and every harvest is a testimony. The apologist can begin with the goodness everyone experiences, and ask where it comes from.

A beginning

“By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible” (Hebrews 11:3). The scientific discovery that the universe had a beginning fits strikingly with this. Things do not come into being from nothing without a cause. So what kind of cause could bring everything into existence? The Christian answer is: the word of God.

The classic arguments

Over two thousand years, Christian thinkers have developed several arguments. The cosmological argument: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore it has a cause beyond itself. The design argument: the universe displays extraordinary order and fitness for life. The moral argument: if there is objective right and wrong — and we all believe there is, especially when we are wronged — then there must be a moral standard beyond humanity. And the ontological argument: the very idea of a greatest possible being implies that such a being exists.

Fine-tuning

In recent decades, the argument from fine-tuning has become especially powerful. Many of the physical constants of the universe, such as the strength of gravity and the forces that bind atoms, fall within extremely narrow ranges that allow life to exist. Many physicists, believers and unbelievers alike, find this striking. John Lennox and William Lane Craig have developed these arguments with care.

These arguments do not prove the Christian God directly. But they strongly suggest that the universe points beyond itself to a mind of extraordinary power and rationality. The apologist’s aim is not to deliver knockout blows, but to unsettle the confidence that the natural world explains itself, and to point to the God who is already there.

Two books

The Reformed tradition, following the Belgic Confession, speaks of two “books” of revelation: creation and Scripture. Creation reveals God’s power, divinity and moral order, enough to leave humanity without excuse. But it cannot reveal the gospel; for that, Scripture is necessary. At their best, the arguments bring a questioner to the threshold of belief in God. The gospel opens the door.

A step at a time

Antony Flew was one of the most influential atheist philosophers of the twentieth century. In 2004 he announced that he had come to believe in God — not as a Christian, but as a theist — chiefly because of the evidence of design in the universe and the complexity of life. He said he had simply followed the argument where it led. Arguments had not made him a Christian, but they had removed the grounds of his atheism. That too is a real outcome of apologetics: a movement from closed certainty to honest enquiry, from which the gospel can be heard.

For reflection

When did creation last move you to wonder? How might you begin a conversation about God from the goodness and order that everyone experiences?

3.title: The Problem of Evil: Suffering and the Good God
3.essay:
No objection to the Christian faith is more emotionally powerful than this: if God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much suffering? It is not only a puzzle for philosophers. It is the cry of the bereaved parent, the cancer patient, the survivor of genocide.

Pastoral first

An apologist who engages this question without tenderness has misunderstood both the question and the questioner. Sometimes the right first response to someone in pain is not an argument but silence, tears and presence. Job’s friends did best when they simply sat with him.

The logical problem

The logical form of the problem, from Epicurus to modern philosophers, argues that evil is incompatible with a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing and perfectly good. If he were all three, there would be no evil; there is evil; so God must lack one of them, or not exist.

Alvin Plantinga’s work showed that it is logically possible for God and evil to coexist, for God may have morally sufficient reasons for permitting evil that we cannot see. Many philosophers, including unbelievers, now accept that the strict logical problem fails. The evidential form — that the sheer amount of evil makes God unlikely — is harder, and needs patient engagement.

Evil points to God

The Christian response is not to explain evil away, which would be dishonest, nor to defend God’s reputation as if he needed us, which would be presumptuous. It is to show that only the Christian worldview can make sense of evil at all. If there is no God, there is no objective evil, only events we happen to dislike. Our very outrage at evil — the conviction that something has gone deeply wrong — assumes a moral order that only a personal God can ground. To say, “I can’t believe in a God who allows this evil,” is to claim that evil is real and objectively wrong. And that claim points back to God.

Where were you?

Job is Scripture’s most searching questioner of divine justice. God’s answer was not an explanation but a revelation of his majesty: “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding” (Job 38:4). And Job’s response was not intellectual satisfaction but worship: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42:5). The encounter with the living God did not answer every question. It transformed the questioner. That is true to the experience of many deep sufferers: what they most needed was not answers but presence.

Not worth comparing

Paul does not minimise suffering; he had endured more than most. But he sets it on an eternal scale: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18). This is not escapism. It is hope. Suffering matters, but it is not the end of the story.

He goes further: “For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). The word preparing means producing. Suffering is not only endured; God works through it to bring about what could not have come any other way. The cross is the supreme example.

Sovereign, not the author

Reformed theology holds that God “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11), yet he is not the author of evil: “God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). The fall brought moral and natural evil into a creation that was very good. God permitted it, and he has not stood apart from its consequences. He entered them in the incarnation, bore them on the cross, and will resolve them in the new creation. God does not always prevent evil; he redeems it.

God’s answer is a person

Finally, the Christian response to suffering is not a philosophical argument but a person. Jesus Christ entered the world of suffering, took its full weight on himself, and defeated it in his resurrection. The cross is not so much an answer to the problem of evil as God’s response to it: personal, self-giving, costly.

Every tear

And the story ends here: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). Not explain every tear, but wipe it away. The resolution is personal and concrete. The new creation will be a world without pain or death, not because these never happened, but because they have been completely overcome. An apologist who knows this has not just an argument but a hope, and hope lived visibly in suffering is one of the most compelling apologetics of all.

Testimonies

Joni Eareckson Tada was paralysed from the neck down in a diving accident at seventeen, and has engaged the problem of evil from the inside for more than fifty years. She has said, in effect, that she would rather be in her wheelchair knowing Jesus than on her feet without him. Corrie ten Boom survived Ravensbrück concentration camp and came out not with atheism but with deeper confidence in God’s love. These are not arguments. They are testimonies. And sometimes a testimony reaches where an argument cannot.

For reflection

How would you respond to a friend in deep pain who asks, “Why did God let this happen?” What would you say, and what would you not say?

4.title: The Resurrection: The Hinge of History
4.essay:
Christianity stands or falls on the resurrection. Paul was blunt: “And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17).

A historical claim

The resurrection is not a metaphor for spiritual renewal or a symbol of hope. It is a historical claim: that a man publicly executed on a Roman cross was physically raised from the dead three days later, appeared to many witnesses, and left his tomb permanently empty. If it is true, it changes everything. If it is false, Christianity collapses.

A testable faith

Paul raises the stakes himself: “And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:14). He does not say the ethical teaching would still be valuable. He stakes everything on a historical event. That is a gift to the apologist. Christianity does not ask for blind faith. It invites honest investigation.

The earliest creed

“For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:3–6).

This is one of the earliest Christian creeds. Paul says he “received” it, and many scholars date it to within a few years of the crucifixion, long before the Gospels were written. Notice the detail: most of the five hundred were still alive. Paul is effectively saying, you can check. The resurrection was not a legend that grew slowly over centuries.

Preached in Jerusalem

At Pentecost, Peter proclaimed, “This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses” (Acts 2:32). He said it in Jerusalem, within weeks of the crucifixion, to crowds who could have walked to the tomb. If the body were there, the claim could have been crushed at once. No one produced it.

The agreed facts

Gary Habermas and Michael Licona have identified a set of facts accepted by most critical historians, including sceptics. Jesus died by crucifixion. His disciples genuinely believed they had seen him risen. Paul, a persecutor of the church, was converted by what he believed was an appearance of the risen Jesus. James, Jesus’ brother and once a sceptic, became a leader of the Jerusalem church. And many historians accept that the tomb was found empty. The question is: what best explains these facts? The resurrection explains them all.

An idea no one would invent

There is also a cultural argument. In first-century Jewish belief, resurrection was something that would happen to all God’s people together, at the end of history. No one expected one man to be raised in the middle of history. The disciples’ claim fitted no existing template; it was not the kind of story anyone would invent. It makes sense only if something extraordinary had actually happened.

Thomas

Thomas is the patron saint of honest doubters. He refused to believe without evidence, and Jesus met him in his doubt, not with rebuke but with invitation: “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe” (John 20:27). Thomas answered, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28) — words a first-century Jew would use only of God himself. The evidence produced not mere agreement but worship. That is the goal of all apologetics.

What it means

The Reformed tradition has always insisted on the bodily, historical resurrection of Jesus, and rejected attempts to turn it into a merely spiritual experience. Christ “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). His resurrection vindicates his atoning work, and it guarantees ours: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

It is also the foundation of apologetics itself. If a man has walked out of death, then the natural order is not the whole story; a Creator exists; his word can be trusted; and the gospel is true.

Investigators who believed

Lee Strobel was an atheist and the legal editor of the Chicago Tribune. When his wife became a Christian, he set out to disprove the resurrection. After nearly two years of investigation and interviews with scholars, he became a Christian, and wrote The Case for Christ. Josh McDowell had a similar journey, from determined sceptic to convinced believer. The resurrection is not a matter of taste or upbringing. It is a historical claim that demands investigation.

For reflection

Why does Paul stake everything on the resurrection? If a sceptical friend asked why you believe Jesus rose, what would you say?

5.title: The Exclusivity of Christ: Is Jesus the Only Way?
5.essay:
In a pluralist culture, the claim that Jesus is the only way to God may be the most offensive thing a Christian can say. It is heard as arrogant and intolerant. Yet it is Jesus’ own claim, and it is a claim of mercy.

A real objection

This objection is often felt most deeply by believers who love and respect people of other faiths, and who are unsure they want to say their friends or relatives are lost. It is born of real love for real people, and it deserves a genuine answer, not a dismissive one. But the answer must also be truthful.

Jesus’ own words

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). This claim is not the church’s invention. Jesus does not say he is a way, or a helpful guide. He says the way, the truth by which every other claim is measured, and the source of life itself.

The exclusive claim is inseparable from the claim about who he is. So a good question to ask an objector is: who do you think Jesus is? If he is who he said — God incarnate, through whom the universe was made, who died for the sins of the world and rose again — then the question changes. It is no longer “Why only Jesus?” but “Is there anyone else who deals with what Jesus deals with?”

No other name

Peter said to the Jerusalem council, “And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). He was not speaking of cultural superiority, but of theological reality. “Under heaven” is universal: not just in our tradition, but anywhere, in any culture, at any time. And the universality of the claim is matched by the universality of the offer.

One mediator, a ransom for all

“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6). There is only one door, but the door is wide open. The scandal is not that there is only one way. The scandal is that the one way is freely and fully sufficient for every person who will come.

Why the cross?

Other religions offer moral teaching, spiritual disciplines and philosophical wisdom, much of it valuable. But none offers what the gospel offers: a God who takes on the guilt of his creatures, bears the full penalty of their rebellion, and gives them his own righteousness as a gift, received by faith.

If there were another way to God, the cross would have been unnecessary. Paul says, “if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (Galatians 2:21). God would not have given up his only Son for nothing. The Reformed tradition, with the whole historic church, has confessed that outside of Christ there is no salvation.

Not to condemn

The verse after the most famous verse in the Bible matters here: “For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). The exclusive claim is a claim of mercy, not of contempt. God sent his Son because he so loved the world. Christ is not a boundary that shuts people out, but a door that is open to all.

Exclusive claims, not exclusive attitudes

The Reformed tradition has always distinguished exclusive claims — Christianity is uniquely true — from exclusive attitudes, treating non-Christians with contempt. The gospel requires the first and forbids the second. We are beggars telling other beggars where to find bread.

The Westminster Confession teaches that people who do not profess the Christian faith cannot be saved by other means, however diligently they live by the light of nature or their own religion. It also recognises that God, by his Spirit, saves some who are incapable of being outwardly called by the preaching of the word, such as infants who die. The church does not presume to know every detail of God’s dealings. It knows that Christ alone saves, and it is commanded to make him known.

Is sincerity enough?

Think of a woman from a devout Hindu family who becomes a Christian. Her relatives ask how she can say that her grandmother, a devoted Hindu, is lost. She answers, “Grandma is in God’s hands, and he is perfectly just and merciful. What I know is what God has done for me, and offers to everyone. The question is not whether Grandma was sincere. It’s whether sincerity can deal with sin. I don’t believe it can. I believe only what Christ did on the cross is enough — and that grace is offered to everyone, including you.” That is faithful, compassionate, honest engagement with the hardest objection.

For reflection

How would you explain to a friend that the exclusivity of Christ is a claim of mercy rather than arrogance? Who do you know who most needs to hear that the door is open?

6.title: Faithful Witness: Apologetics as a Way of Life
6.essay:
Apologetics is not only for philosophers and theologians. It is the calling of every believer who lives among people who do not yet know Christ, which means all of us. And the most powerful apologetic is not an argument. It is a life.

The final apologetic

Jesus prayed for his people “that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me” (John 17:21). And he said, “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

Francis Schaeffer called this the final apologetic: the visible love and unity of the Christian community. Arguments can be countered and evidence disputed. But a community of people who love one another across every human barrier, who forgive when the world would retaliate, who give when the culture hoards, who face death with peace, and who are joyful in ways the world cannot explain, demands an explanation. The explanation is Jesus. An apologist who neglects the local church has missed where the greatest argument for the gospel is made.

A faithful witness

Arguments still matter. But they are most effective when they come from within a life that is itself an argument for the gospel. A faithful witness knows why they believe what they believe. They listen before they speak. They ask good questions instead of delivering lectures. They meet people in their real pain before engaging their intellectual objections. They pray for the people they talk with. And they trust that God is more committed to the salvation of their sceptical friend than they are.

Ambassadors

“Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). An ambassador represents a King and carries the King’s message. And the message is a plea. The tone of Christian apologetics should finally be this: not triumphant, not contemptuous, not merely clever, but imploring. We want people to be reconciled to the God who loves them.

The cross remains

“For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:22–24).

Every culture finds its own reason to stumble over a crucified Messiah. The apologist removes as many false obstacles as possible, but cannot remove the cross, because the cross is the message. A God who dies, a King who is crucified, power revealed in weakness: this is the very thing the Spirit uses to save. The last word of apologetics is not a syllogism but a proclamation: Christ crucified.

Beautiful feet

Apologetics ends where it must: in proclamation. “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14). And Paul adds, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” (Romans 10:15). Every cleared obstacle is in service of one thing: that someone might hear the gospel and believe.

The Spirit converts

The Spirit’s work in conversion is the apologist’s great comfort and great caution. Comfort, because the Spirit can use any argument, question or moment of honest encounter to open a heart. Caution, because no argument, however compelling, converts anyone. “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8).

So apologetics is a ministry of means, not mechanisms. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). We clear obstacles; the Spirit opens eyes. That frees us from feeling that every conversation must end in conversion, and lets us be faithful rather than frantic.

Seeing everything else

C. S. Lewis is perhaps the best-known Christian apologist of the twentieth century. He came to faith through reading, conversation and the friendship of believers, including a long late-night talk with J. R. R. Tolkien and Hugo Dyson. He spent the rest of his life clearing obstacles for others, through Mere Christianity, The Problem of Pain, Miracles, The Screwtape Letters and the Narnia stories: arguments, imagination and story all serving the truth. His approach was never to bludgeon but to invite.

He wrote, “I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen: not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.” That is the goal of apologetics: not to argue people into faith, but to help them see everything else in the light of Christ.

The last word

Every argument and every answer serves one announcement: Christ has died for sinners and been raised for their justification, and he has promised, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

For reflection

Is your life, and your church’s life together, an argument for the gospel? Who is one person you could pray for, listen to and gently witness to this month?
